title: Everest BatchStream POC — Latency & Cost Diary
body:
Purpose:
This is the working diary and evaluation notes for the Everest customer POC. Goal: validate the BatchStream serving mode (micro-batching with streaming output) for a mixed workload that has both short interactive queries and longer generation jobs. We need to quantify median/tail latency, throughput at different concurrency points, and per-request cost implications across a few deployment knobs (batch window, kv-cache warmup, quantization profile, and model fallbacks).

Quick summary findings (top line):
- Stable median latency for short queries (<= 64 tokens) at 15ms–28ms depending on batch-window and warm cache.
- 99th percentile for bursty mixed traffic spikes to 420ms when KV cache hit rate drops < 40% (cold cluster or after scale event).
- Throughput: sustained 1100 qps on a 4xA100 config when using adaptive batching (max batch 256, dynamic window), drops to ~760 qps with conservative fixed window (10ms).
- Cost per 1k requests (mixed profile) varies 34% between aggressive quant+batch and baseline FP16 config.
- Recommended production config: adaptive batch window + pre-warm KV cache + quant-8 profile for user-facing tier, keep FP16 fallback for highest-quality model variants.

Test setup and assumptions:
- Customer workload: 60% short queries (<= 64 tokens), 30% medium (65–256 tokens), 10% long (>= 257 tokens, streaming expected).
- Hardware: test cluster of 4xA100 (40GB) per node; experiments run both single-node and distributed with 2 nodes.
- Model: OpenLarge-v2 (~25B) — supported FP16 and quantized int8 variants.
- Serving mode: BatchStream (micro-batch aggregation period configurable 1–20ms with dynamic window) implemented on Redwood runtime staging branch se/batchstream-2027.
- Key factors instrumented: batch window, max batch size, KV cache policy (LRU TTL 30m vs persistent), quantization profile, coldstart state (empty KV and model caches), request prioritization (interactive vs background).

Workloads executed:
1) Synthetic steady-state mixed: 800 qps steady, mix as above. Ran 20-minute runs to measure steady throughput and tail.
2) Spike ramp: steady 200 qps then ramp to 2k qps over 30s, hold 60s, then drop. Observed auto-scaling behavior and tail latency.
3) Cold cluster: restart nodes and replay a 5-minute traffic pattern to observe warmup.
4) Streaming-heavy run: 100 qps of long requests to validate streaming latency and backpressure.

Detailed observations and measurements:
A) Batch window tuning:
- 2ms window (aggressive): median latency for short queries 15–18ms, but variability in 95/99p for medium requests due to increased batching of long tokens; throughput highest.
- 10ms window (conservative): median jumps to 24–28ms for short queries but 95/99p improves when KV misses occur because larger windows allow better packing and amortize kernel launches.
- Dynamic/adaptive window (based on incoming QPS and current batch fullness) produced the best balance: median ~20ms, 99p ~120ms in steady-state. Adaptive also reduced cost by ~10% over fixed 10ms.

B) KV cache warmup and tail effects:
- KV cache hit rate is the single largest driver of tail latency. With warm KV (hit rate > 85%) 99p for short/medium requests remains < 100ms.
- After scale events / node restarts KV hit rate drops below 40% and we observed 99p spikes to 350–420ms in mixed spike runs.
- Pre-warm strategy (synthetic warm traffic + persistent local checkpointing) recovers hit-rate within 3–6 minutes for typical traces. Documented TTL=30m LRU and a small warmup loader script that replays most frequent prefixes reduced the tail by ~60% during scale events.

C) Quantization vs quality/cost tradeoffs:
- int8 quant reduces per-token GPU time by ~22% in micro-batch heavy runs (best case). Combined with adaptive batching this yielded the 34% cost reduction cited above.
- Quality regression for edge-case completions observed in the medium/long set — customers must validate task-specific evals before applying int8 globally. Proposed pattern: apply int8 for interactive tier, and keep FP16 for background generation/analytic jobs.

D) Coldstart behavior and warm pools:
- Cold model loads add ~180–260ms depending on model variant; KV cold adds 70–120ms.
- Warm pools (kept-hot reserved instances) eliminate model cold penalty but increase baseline cost. For Everest use-case (SLA 200ms 95p), warm pools + adaptive batching is required during predictable business hours; outside peak, autoscale with graceful pre-warm.

E) Burst handling and graceful degradation:
- During 2k qps spikes, BatchStream runtime started prioritizing interactive flags (configured per-request). With priority routing we kept 95p for interactive under 300ms while background jobs' latency degraded proportionally.
- Fallback policy to smaller, cheaper model variant worked well: when queue backlog exceeds threshold (configured as 2s of backlog), route 20% of background long requests to a quantized smaller model; observed ~48% cost saving during sustained bursts with 2–4% observed drop in task-specific BLEU-like metric for those offloaded jobs.

Cost modeling notes (per 1k mixed requests):
- Baseline FP16 (fixed 10ms): $2.86 per 1k
- Adaptive batching + int8: $1.89 per 1k
- Warm pools add a fixed infra premium ~12–18% depending on reservation level but reduce tail-mitigation engineering cost and risk.
- Cost numbers are system-level approximations including GPU runtime, amortized model load, and simple infra overhead; does not include network egress or storage.

Failures, anomalies, and root-cause hypotheses:
- Anomalous 99p spike on 2027-11-12 run: seen only on node B; kernel profiler showed occasional CUDA kernel serialization caused by memory fragmentation after repeated large long-generation jobs. Root cause hypothesis: long-tail memory allocator fragmentation + aggressive KV eviction due to TTL flush. Mitigations: schedule periodic defrag epoch (off-peak), increase KV shard size, reduce eviction frequency during high-load windows.

Operational recommendations for Everest POC next phase:
1) Adopt adaptive batch window with dynamic max-batch cap of 256 and enforcement of request priority.
2) Implement persistent KV snapshots for fast warmup plus a small synthetic warm-replay during scale events.
3) Roll quant-8 to interactive tier only after passing customer-specific eval sets (quality gates).
4) Keep FP16 fallback and implement automatic fallback routing when quality/regression monitoring flags a drop.
5) For production SLA 95p <= 200ms: use warm pools during business hours sized to handle expected peak QPS headroom (recommended 25% buffer).
6) Add a periodic maintenance defrag window to mitigate kernel serialization anomaly.

Open questions and action items:
- Customer to provide a representative evaluation prompt set for quality gating (action: Product/SE request).
- Confirm acceptable cost-saving target vs quality delta for offloading to smaller model variants (action: GTM/customer decision).
- Engineering to prototype persistent KV shard resizing and reheating workflow (owner: Chen Wu, due 2027-11-22).
- Run extended 72-hour soak with production-representative diurnal pattern (owner: Liam Ortega, scheduled start 2027-11-20).

Appendix: short experiment log (dates and quick notes)
- 2027-11-08: baseline steady-state runs (4xA100 single node), collected latency histograms, kernel traces.
- 2027-11-09: adaptive batching commit tested, throughput + cost improvements clear.
- 2027-11-10: coldstart runs and KV warmup script iterated. Noted persistent spike behavior after restarts.
- 2027-11-12: anomaly observed on node B — kernel serialization traces captured.
- 2027-11-14: quant-8 evaluation against internal eval set; cost win strong but edge-case regressions flagged.

Contact and follow-up: Priya Mahadevan (SE lead) — priya@redwood.ai. For infra/API changes open JIRA-7891 and link proposed PR github.com/redwood/benchmarks/pull/456.

Notes to self: keep this diary updated after the 72-hour soak. Capture comparative token-level cost where possible (we currently report per-request only). Add more granular per-route dashboards in Console: fill missing dashboards for KV hit heatmap and model-fallback incidence.
